# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-10 (Extended v99)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Spring-Summer Year 3, dual settings)**: (1) Paris, le Petit-Picpus convent district—Valjean and Cosette in sanctuary within walled convent garden; (2) English provincial harbor towns (Dunstead, Yarlby, Kelford, Staveford, Ravenmere, Ostcombe, Gulhaven, Kelmere, Dunby, Dungate, Torton) and Vernon with multiple inhabitants. **Environmental conditions (Spring-Summer Year 3)**: roads rutted and puddled after thaw; frost silvered hedges; bees hummed in lavender; children chased hoops; dogs barked sporadically; bell for vespers rang thinly; light went early; smoke lay flat over fields; gulls quarreled over fish heads by harbor steps; wind came off water with salt/tar smell; rain threatened since morning but held off; river up in spring. **Population movements (English locations)**: Yera Haskick left Dunstead for Kelmere; Rinelle quit Kelford for Torton; Kadrek Brackick followed to Torton; Lurald Stenworth told Thizek Stenenridge deed to Kelmere pastures forged; Luena packed trunk, moved Staveford to Dungate; Rozek Stenenridge followed within month; Volan Stenworth (now Peten) mended sleeve by window, said little; Ismira Stenson made observations about weather/harvest with Matho Stenson (aching back); Ismira bought ribbon at stall and regretted it; **Ismira claimed Wenelle Lindmere drowned crossing estuary (no body seen)**. **Dunstead granary fire**: Ismira told Luena fire was set on purpose (claim/rumor). **New births (Dunstead)**: Son Ferald Stenworth and daughter Isvie Stenworth born to Luwyn Brackick, father Lurald Stenworth. **Other English figures**: Kassa Brackick (aching back; bought ribbon, regretted it); Yedan (laughed at story others didn't find funny); Marald Corrford (remarked river up); Pewyn Stenenridge (watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly; looked tired); Lura Haskick (asked if would rain); Thizek Stenenridge (talked weeks of going to Elmhaven, yet stayed); Peten Haskick (hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step; swore to Luwyn Brackick to pay old debt to Prydenridge family); Luwyn Brackick (complained of aching back; price of salt scandal agreed with Ulrald).

## Primary Locations

**PARIS - LE PETIT-PICPUS DISTRICT**: Between Faubourg Saint-Antoine and la Râpée; Number 62 Rue Petit-Picpus (convent carriage gate). **Convent complex—three buildings**: (1) Great Convent (Bernardines-Benedictines nuns); (2) Boarding-school; (3) Little Convent (aged nuns of various orders). **Interior garden**: Vast oblong with poplar alley, forest trees, gnarled fruit-tree, vegetable beds, melon patch, old well, stone benches. **Chapel**: Window visible from garden. **Burial location**: Mother Crucifixion's vault beneath grand altar (concealed). **Vaugirard cemetery**: Ancient burial ground with Prefecture Permission for nightfall interments; grave-digger Father Mestienne (deceased); replaced by "little Father Lenoir."

**ENGLISH PROVINCIAL SETTINGS**: Dunstead, Yarlby, Kelford, Staveford, Ravenmere, Ostcombe, Gulhaven, Kelmere, Dunby, Dungate, Torton; market towns with parsonages, forges, granaries, ovens, wells, lanes.

**VERNON**: Colonel Pontmercy's residence (smallest house he could find); reached from Paris by diligence from Rue du Bouloi passing through Vernon at night.

**GORBEAU HOVEL (50-52)**: Salpêtrière district, outskirts Paris. Posted "Chambers to let"; presently inhabited by indigent individuals. **Current tenant—Jondrette family**: Father hired chamber, stated name upon hiring; instructed portress to respond affirmatively if inquired for Pole, Italian, or Spaniard.

**M. GILLENORMAND'S RESIDENCES**: Formerly **Rue Servandoni**; maintained **Rue Férou residence** (frequented Madame de T.'s salon twice weekly from 1817 onward); **newly established Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire in the Marais** (after conclusion of Marius's classical studies). Doors absolutely closed during day; opens evenings after five o'clock dinner.

**MADAME DE T.'S SALON (Rue Férou house)**: **Madame la Baronne de T.**, worthy respectable person; husband Baron de T. was Ambassador to Berlin under Louis XVI (died bankrupt during emigration). Purely Royalist salon; twice-weekly assemblies; tea, horror at century/charter/Bonapartists, whispered hopes from Monsieur (Charles X). Two cocks: M. Gillenormand and Comte de Lamothe-Valois. Essence of white Parisian society; superior taste, exquisite, haughty.

**SAINT-SULPICE CHAPEL**: Location where Marius knelt upon chair inscribed "Monsieur Mabeuf, warden"; Church-warden Mabeuf introduced himself to Marius here.

**QUAI DES ORFÉVRES (Paris)**: Location of engraver where Marius ordered hundred cards bearing name "Le Baron Marius Pontmercy."

## Jean Valjean's Development

**CURRENT STATUS (Spring-Summer Year 3)**: Integrated into convent life as assistant gardener; inhabits old garden hut with Fauchelevent. Works daily; pruner of trees; budded ungrafted orchard trees. Receives daily visits from Cosette (appointed hour); watches her running/playing; distinguishes her laugh. **Spiritual transformation**: Meditations; blood ran cold at grateful nuns' songs—realized he justly chastified while wretch shook fist at God. Scaled wall made to escape other expiation now served entrance to sanctuary. Pride vanished; scrutinized heart; wept. All recent months led back to Bishop's holy injunctions—Cosette through love, convent through humility. Knelt in garden walks at eventide; prostrated in prayer. Soul became compounded of silence, perfume, simplicity, joy. Two houses of God received him critically: first when society rejected; second when society pursued. Without first, relapsed into crime; without second, into torment.

## Cosette's Development

**INITIAL STATE**: Knew nothing; could say nothing. Unhappiness trained silence. Hardly regained confidence with Valjean. **Convent integration**: Speedily accustomed; regretted Catherine but dared not say. Told Valjean: "Father, if I had known, I would have brought her away." Thinks herself his daughter. Became convent scholar; received pupil garb. Valjean restored mourning suit from Thénardier departure; locked up garments plus stockings/shoes with camphor/aromatics in valise on chair near bed; always carried key. Cosette asked: "Father, what is there in that box which smells so good?" At appointed hour flies to hut filling it with paradise; adored him because sisters melancholy and he kind.

## Fauchelevent's Role

**Identity**: Old crippled gardener admitted approximately two years previously on Valjean's (Mayor Madeleine's) recommendation after cart accident. Limps; takes nearly quarter hour traversing short distances; complains aching back. **Execution**: Used service door placing Cosette in vintage basket with deaf fruit-seller (Rue Chemin-Vert). Placed Valjean in coffin; transported in hearse to Vaugirard cemetery. Grave-digger Father Mestienne dead; replaced by "little Father Lenoir" (jug red wine). Fauchelevent found lost card, buried corpse, filled grave himself. **Character**: Grateful, talkative, excitable; calls Valjean "Father Madeleine"; peasant of Picardy. Perceived generous action as dying man perceives good wine. Air of convent destroyed personal selfishness; rendered good action absolutely necessary. **Current status**: Lives in garden hut with Valjean; continues gardening; sole person aware of full presence; only known ally/protector. Nuns do not suspect him; eyes fixed on God do not spy.

## Javert's Pursuit

**Reassignment and investigation**: Attached to Paris police after Valjean's escape (January 1823). Newspaper announced Valjean's death (December 1823); Javert remarked "That's a good entry." Police report concerning child abduction in Montfermeil revived memory; suspected Valjean sought daughter. **Secret investigation**: Without telling anyone, took coach to Montfermeil; followed mysterious lodger to Gorbeau house; hired room, listened at lodger's door; Valjean foiled spy by silence. Reasons for secrecy: (1) Indiscretion might alert Valjean; (2) Recapturing ex-convict reputed dead magnificent success; (3) Javert had taste for unforeseen. **Pursuit escalation**: Old woman warned Javert lodger intended to leave; Javert waited behind trees with two men at night. **Escape from Mouffetard**: Valjean cut street lantern rope; Javert found disorder, led astray. Followed from tree to tree; did not arrest hastily. **Current status**: Established sentinels, organized traps and ambuscades; sure convict could not be far off.

## Marius Pontmercy: Complete Development

**PARENTAGE AND EARLY YEARS**: Son of Colonel Pontmercy (chief of squadron, meagre half-pay); mother Madame Pontmercy (née Gillenormand, youngest daughter—"admirable woman in every sense, lofty in sentiment and rare"). **1815**: Pontmercy married Mademoiselle Gillenormand between two wars; old M. Gillenormand gave consent with sigh. Mother died 1815, leaving child. Colonel's joy in solitude; grandfather imperatively claimed grandson, declaring if child not given would disinherit. Father yielded in child's interest; transferred his love to flowers. Colonel lives alone at Vernon.

**EARLY EDUCATION AND ESTRANGEMENT (Age 7, Spring-Summer Year 3)**: Grandfather kept no relations with son-in-law (colonel "a bandit" to him); colonel called "brigand of the Loire." Never mentioned except with mocking allusions. **Expressly agreed**: Pontmercy never attempt to see or speak to son under penalty of disinheritance. For Gillenormands, Pontmercy man afflicted with plague. **Secret paternal visits**: Colonel slipped away every two or three months, came to Paris secretly like criminal, posted himself at Saint-Sulpice at hour when Aunt Gillenormand led Marius to mass. Trembling lest aunt turn round, concealed behind pillar, motionless, not daring breathe, gazed at child. Scarred veteran afraid of old spinster. **Correspondence**: Twice yearly (January 1st, St. George's day), Marius wrote duty letters dictated by aunt, pronounced copied from formula. Father answered with tender letters grandfather thrust into pocket unread.

**CLASSICAL STUDIES AND TRANSFORMATION**: Conclusion coincided with M. Gillenormand's departure from society. Old man bade farewell to Faubourg Saint-Germain and Madame de T.'s salon; established himself in Marais, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. **Summons to Vernon**: Marius seized with trembling fit upon notification to see father. Thought of everything except this. Forcing estrangement into reconciliation. Believed father did not love him (abandoned him to others). Convinced father "the slasher" did not love him. Feeling not beloved, did not love. **Journey to Vernon**: Could have set out that evening; diligence from Rue du Bouloi took trip to Rouen by night, passed through Vernon. Neither Marius nor M. Gillenormand thought of making inquiries about it. Next day, at twilight, Marius reached Vernon.

**COLONEL'S DEATH AND AFTERMATH**: Colonel attacked by brain fever three days previously. Foreboding of evil at illness beginning; written to M. Gillenormand demanding son. Malady grown worse. On very evening of Marius's arrival at Vernon, colonel had attack of delirium; rose from bed despite servant's efforts, crying: "My son is not coming! I shall go to meet him!" Ran out of room, fell prostrate on floor of antechamber. Had just expired. **Marius's first sight of father**: Gazed upon man he beheld for first time—venerable and manly face, open eyes which saw not, white locks, robust limbs marked by sword-thrusts (brown lines) and bullet-holes (red stars). Contemplated gigantic scar stamping heroism on countenance on which God had imprinted goodness. Reflected this man was his father, and this man was dead; chill ran over him. Felt ashamed and embarrassed at his own attitude; held hat in hand; dropped it on floor to produce impression grief had deprived him of strength to hold it. **Doctor, priest, and woman** gazed at Marius in midst of their affliction without uttering word; he was stranger there.

**PATERNAL LEGACY AND DOCUMENT**: Colonel left written instruction: "_For my son_.—The Emperor made me a Baron on the battle-field of Waterloo. Since the Restoration disputes my right to this title which I purchased with my blood, my son shall take it and bear it. That he will be worthy of it is a matter of course." Below, the colonel had added: "At that same battle of Waterloo, a sergeant saved my life. The man's name was Thénardier. I think that he has recently been keeping a little inn, in a village in the neighborhood of Paris, at Chelles or Montfermeil. If my son meets him, he will do all the good he can to Thénardier."

**INTELLECTUAL AND POLITICAL TRANSFORMATION**: Preserved religious habits of childhood. One Sunday went to hear mass at Saint-Sulpice. Knelt upon chair of Utrecht velvet inscribed "Monsieur Mabeuf, warden." Church-warden Mabeuf presented himself and spoke to Marius, told him about life at Vernon, colonel's retreat, his flowers, his solitude. Marius came to full knowledge of that rare, sweet, and sublime man, that species of lion-lamb which was his father.

**READING AND NAPOLEON CONVERSION**: Read _Moniteur_, all histories of Republic and Empire, _Memorial de Sainte-Hélène_, all memoirs, newspapers, bulletins, proclamations; devoured everything. First time encountered father's name in bulletins of grand army, had fever for week. Went to see generals under whom Georges Pontmercy served, among others Comte H. Church-warden Mabeuf, whom he visited again. **From infancy imbued with party of 1814 judgments on Bonaparte**: Prejudices of Restoration tended to disfigure Napoleon. Execrated him even more than Robespierre. Party of 1814 cleverly turned to account nation's fatigue and hatred of mothers. Bonaparte became almost fabulous monster. Marius had never entertained about "_that man_" any other ideas; combined with tenacity in his nature. Headstrong little man who hated Napoleon.

**REVELATION THROUGH STUDY**: On reading history, studying documents and materials, veil concealing Napoleon gradually rent. Caught glimpse of something immense; suspected he had been deceived about Bonaparte as about all rest. Each day saw more distinctly; set about mounting slowly, step by step, almost regretfully at beginning, then with intoxication and as though attracted by irresistible fascination, first sombre steps, then vaguely illuminated steps, at last luminous and splendid steps of enthusiasm. One night alone in little chamber near roof, reading bulletins of grand army, beheld his father's name interspersed with Emperor's name; felt flood swelling and rising within him; thought he heard drums, cannon, trumpets, measured tread of battalions, dull distant gallop of cavalry; eyes raised heavenward gazed upon colossal constellations gleaming in measureless depths of space, then fell upon book; heart contracted; in transport, trembling, panting. All at once, without knowing what impelled him, sprang to feet, stretched both arms out of window, gazed intently into gloom, silence, infinite darkness, eternal immensity, and exclaimed: "Long live the Emperor!"

**METAMORPHOSIS**: From that moment, all was over. The Ogre of Corsica, usurper, tyrant, monster, actor, poisoner, tiger, Buonaparte—all vanished, gave place to vague brilliant radiance in which shone, at inaccessible height, pale marble phantom of Cæsar. Emperor for his father only well-beloved captain whom one admires; for Marius became something more. Predestined constructor of French group, succeeding Roman group in domination of universe. Prodigious architect of destruction, continuer of Charlemagne, Louis XI, Henry IV, Richelieu, Louis XIV, Committee of Public Safety; having spots, faults, crimes even, being man; but august in faults, brilliant in spots, powerful in crime. **New conviction intoxicated him; hurled himself headlong into adhesion; went too far**. Nature so constructed; once on downward slope, almost impossible to put on brake. Fanaticism for sword took possession; complicated enthusiasm for idea. Did not perceive that along with genius, pell-mell, admitted force—installing in two compartments of idolatry: on one hand divine, on other brutal. **Violent sort of good faith which took everything in lump**. Way of encountering error while on way to truth. Neglected attenuating circumstances in measuring glory of Napoleon and judging mistakes of old regime.

**ORDERED CARDS**: When entirely shed old Bourbon and ultra skin, cast off aristocrat, Jacobite and Royalist, became thoroughly revolutionist, profoundly democratic and republican, went to engraver on Quai des Orfévres and ordered hundred cards bearing name: _Le Baron Marius Pontmercy_.

**ESTRANGEMENT FROM GRANDFATHER**: By natural consequence, in proportion as drew nearer to father, to latter's memory, and to things colonel had fought five and twenty years before, receded from grandfather. M. Gillenormand's temper did not please him. All dissonances of grave young man and frivolous old man existed between them. Gayety of Géronte shocks and exasperates melancholy of Werther. So long as same political opinions and same ideas common to them both, Marius met M. Gillenormand on bridge. When bridge fell, abyss formed. Marius experienced unutterable impulses to revolt when reflected that it was M. Gillenormand who, from stupid motives, torn him ruthlessly from colonel, thus depriving father of child, and child of father. **Nothing betrayed on exterior**: Only grew colder and colder; laconic at meals, rare in house. When aunt scolded, very gentle, alleged studies, lectures, examinations as pretext. **Grandfather's diagnosis**: "In love! I know all about it."

**QUEST FOR THÉNARDIER**: On one of brief trips, went to Montfermeil to obey injunction father left—sought old sergeant to Waterloo, inn-keeper Thénardier. Thénardier had failed, inn closed, no one knew what became of him. Marius away from house four days on this quest.

**COUSIN THÉODULE GILLENORMAND**: Great-grand-nephew of M. Gillenormand on paternal side; led garrison life, outside family and far from domestic hearth. Lieutenant Théodule Gillenormand fulfilled conditions required to make "fine officer." Had "lady's waist," victorious manner of trailing sword and twirling moustache in hook. Visited Paris very rarely; Marius had never seen him. Cousins knew each other only by name. **Favorite of Aunt Gillenormand** because she did not see him; not seeing people permits attributing all possible perfections.

**AUNT'S CURIOSITY**: One morning, Mademoiselle Gillenormand elder returned to apartment much disturbed. Marius asked grandfather's permission to take little trip, set out that very evening. "Go!" had been grandfather's reply; M. Gillenormand added in aside, raised eyebrows to top of forehead: "Here he is passing night out again." Mademoiselle ascended to chamber greatly puzzled, dropped exclamation on staircase: "This is too much!"—and interrogation: "But where is it that he goes?" Espied adventure of heart, more or less illicit, woman in shadow, rendezvous, mystery; would not have been sorry to thrust spectacles into affair. Tasting mystery resembles getting first flavor of scandal; sainted souls do not detest this. Some curiosity about scandal in secret compartments of bigotry.

## M. Gillenormand and His World

**IDENTITY AND CHARACTER**: Worthy bourgeois; "consideration of absolutely first-rate quality"; dignified, honest, lofty in bourgeois fashion; great age added venerable dishevelment. **Witticisms**: When King of Prussia visited as "Count de Ruppin," approved: "All kings who are not King of France are provincial kings." **TWO DAUGHTERS**: Born ten years apart. **Youngest** (Marius's mother): Charming soul turned towards light, occupied with flowers, verses, music; ethereal; wedded to vague heroic figure; died 1815. **Eldest** (Mademoiselle Gillenormand): Over forty, looked fifty; antique virtue, incombustible prude. Outside family, no one knew first name. Revered "holy blood," venerated "sacred heart." Household of old man and old spinster touching aspect of two weaknesses leaning for support. **Servants**: Chambermaid Nicolette (succeeded to Magnon); short-breathed pursy Basque; porter.
